result.question: I need to know whether the fault in Transformer 1 at MAIN is getting worse or changing character. Run a DGA fault classification on the first and the last complete oil sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. Tell me each sample's fault class and confidence. Then tell me whether the class moved toward a higher-energy or higher-temperature fault, for example PD to D1, or T1 to T2/T3. If the two classifications disagree, explain which one you trust more and why, based on the absolute gas levels and not just the ratios. Then recommend one specific next check, such as a confirmatory resample, an OLTC compartment sample or an electrical test. Count a sample as complete only if all five gases are non-null. If there is only one complete sample in the window, classify that one alone and say that no progression can be judged.
result.answer:
I couldn't get the tool classifications. The DGA classification tool (`interpret_dga`) returned "LLM unavailable" three times, so I worked out the classes by hand from the raw gas values using the IEC 60599 ratio limits. The confidence ratings below are my own judgement, not a model score.

**Samples in the window:** all 4 daily samples (Jan 15–18) have all five gases, so all count as complete. First = 2024-01-15, last = 2024-01-18.

| Sample | H₂ | CH₄ | C₂H₆ | C₂H₄ | C₂H₂ | C₂H₂/C₂H₄ | CH₄/H₂ | C₂H₄/C₂H₆ | Fault class | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-01-15 | 2845 | 7406 | 5467 | 16684 | 7 | 0.0004 | 2.60 | 3.05 | T2 (300–700 °C), near the T3 boundary | Medium |
| 2024-01-18 | 2900 | 7350 | 5450 | 16600 | 7 | 0.0004 | 2.53 | 3.05 | T2 (300–700 °C), near the T3 boundary | Medium |

The confidence is only medium because C₂H₄/C₂H₆ is about 3.05 in both samples. That is below the IEC T2/T3 boundary of 4. But it is just above the Rogers boundary of 3, which would call it T3 (over 700 °C). Duval Triangle 1 also puts it in T3 (about 69% C₂H₄, 31% CH₄, 0.03% C₂H₂). So the most accurate description is a high-temperature thermal fault on the T2/T3 border, roughly 600–700 °C or hotter.

**Progression:** there is no shift toward a higher-energy or higher-temperature fault. Both samples give the same class with almost the same ratios, and the two middle samples match too (C₂H₄/C₂H₆ of 3.04–3.06). Acetylene stays at 6–8 ppm, so there is no move toward arcing (D1/D2). Gas levels changed by only −1% to +2% over three days, which is within normal repeat-sample variation. So the fault is not getting worse or changing character over this window.

**Agreement:** the two samples agree, so there is nothing to choose between. The absolute levels support the thermal diagnosis:
- Ethylene is about 16,600 ppm, methane about 7,400 ppm, ethane about 5,450 ppm and hydrogen about 2,850 ppm. These are many times normal levels, so this is not ratio noise from trace gases.
- Acetylene at about 7 ppm is small next to about 16,600 ppm of ethylene. It points to a very hot thermal spot, not an arc.
- Nothing is rising. That means either a stable active hot spot or gas left over from an earlier event, and the DGA alone cannot tell which.

**Recommended next check:** a DC winding resistance test at every tap position, compared phase to phase. A thermal fault at around 700 °C with this much ethylene and little acetylene is most often an overheating contact. Likely spots are a tap-selector contact, a bolted lead joint or a bushing connection. This test can find and locate a high-resistance joint.

The acetylene is too low relative to hydrogen and ethylene to suggest oil leaking from the tap-changer compartment. So I'd do this electrical test before taking an OLTC compartment sample.
